dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: karaṅkiṇyā krodhanayā bhairavyā lelihānayā | khecaryā dṛṣṭikāle ca parāvāptiḥ prakāśate ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
dharana.rendering: Through the seals (mudrā) called karaṅkiṇī, krodhanā, bhairavī, lelihānā and khecarī, at the moment of seeing, the supreme attainment shines forth.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh, following Lakshmanjoo, takes dṛṣṭikāla as 'at the time of practice' and describes each mudrā: karaṅkiṇī views the world as a mere skeleton and the body as dissolved in the highest space; krodhanā is a tense, tight disposition; bhairavī keeps the eyes fixed outward without blinking while attention turns inward; lelihānā 'tastes' the universe as one's own I-consciousness; khecarī has several forms, including turning the tongue back toward the palate, and in its highest form is remaining in Śiva-consciousness. Wallis notes that the Sanskrit commentaries are needed to understand the verse and counts the five mudrās as five yuktis (Y49–53).
dharana.technique_name: The Five Seals at the Moment of Seeing
dharana.instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. For a gentle gaze practice, use Door 057 or Door 061.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 77 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The classical map is five named seals, each a way of holding attention at the moment of perception. Drawn faint: studied, not drilled.
geometry.svg_hint: five small faint marks in a row, each labelled with a seal name; drawn faint to signal observe-only
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Five seals (described)
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: five classical ways of sealing attention in the moment of seeing. A list to understand, not an exercise. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: wherever the breath naturally ends; this door places nothing on the breath
breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Study the verse; let the body simply rest while you do
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.primary: Understanding the five named seals and why the verse needs commentary
attention.secondary: If sitting with anything, only the soft gaze of Door 057

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: Through the seals (mudrā) called karaṅkiṇī, krodhanā, bhairavī, lelihānā and khecarī, at the moment of seeing, the supreme attainment shines forth.
adiyogi.method_summary: Classical method: five seals (karaṅkiṇī, krodhanā, bhairavī, lelihānā, khecarī), each described only in commentary, are practised at the moment of perception, and the supreme attainment shines forth. Observe-only in this school: read and understand it. For a gentle gaze practice, use Door 057 or Door 061.

honesty.disclosure: Door 054 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 54 (verse 77) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.

historical/observe_only: The verse names five esoteric seals (mudrā) known only from commentary; some involve physical techniques (a tense, tight disposition; turning the tongue back toward the palate; an unblinking fixed gaze) and they belong to initiatory lineages. Taught as text to understand, not as a class drill.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. The physical forms of these seals (tongue-turning, sustained unblinking gaze, tense holding) are not taught by this school. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. These seals are esoteric and commentary-dependent, and some forms (tongue-turning, sustained unblinking gaze, tense holding) can strain the body. For a gentle gaze practice, use Door 057 or Door 061.
